power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: An advanced LAMP assay targeting the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was developed and validated using clinical and foodborne S. aureus isolates.
Reference strains, including both methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant S. aureus, were used to evaluate and optimize assay performance.
With the newly designed ID16 LAMP primer set, the detection limit for mecA was 15 fg/µL of total genomic DNA, equivalent to 5 copies/µL, and the assay turnaround time was only 25 min.
All mecA-positive isolates identified by conventional qPCR were successfully detected by the LAMP assay.
Overall, the developed LAMP method provides a rapid, highly specific, and sensitive alternative for mecA detection.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a critical global health challenge, contributing to millions of deaths annually and imposing a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and societies worldwide [1, 2].
text.formatted: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a critical global health challenge, contributing to millions of deaths annually and imposing a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and societies worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Resistant bacteria are primarily transmitted through three major reservoirs: community-associated pathways (person-to-person spread), healthcareassociated environments (usually via contaminated surfaces and medical equipment), and livestock-associated routes (predominantly through food products of animal origin).

In those reservoirs, AMR genes can be spread from resistant strains to sensitive ones through the horizontal gene transfer mechanisms such as conjugation, transduction, and transformation, often facilitated by mobile genetic elements like integrons and transposons [3].
text.formatted: In those reservoirs, AMR genes can be spread from resistant strains to sensitive ones through the horizontal gene transfer mechanisms such as conjugation, transduction, and transformation, often facilitated by mobile genetic elements like integrons and transposons <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, an extensive use of antibiotics will favour the emergence of resistance by creating a selective pressure environment [4].
text.formatted: Moreover, an extensive use of antibiotics will favour the emergence of resistance by creating a selective pressure environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium, usually commensal, as part of the normal microbiota of the body and can be found in nares, skin, and the gastrointestinal tract [5].
text.formatted: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium, usually commensal, as part of the normal microbiota of the body and can be found in nares, skin, and the gastrointestinal tract <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: However, S. aureus can be opportunistic pathogen leading to pneumonia, endocarditis, and sepsis, among others [6].
text.formatted: However, S. aureus can be opportunistic pathogen leading to pneumonia, endocarditis, and sepsis, among others <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, group of strains of S. aureus that are resistant to methicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics i.e., MRSA is one of the leading causes of healthcare-associated and community-acquired infections, according to WHO [7, 8].
text.formatted: Furthermore, group of strains of S. aureus that are resistant to methicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics i.e., MRSA is one of the leading causes of healthcare-associated and community-acquired infections, according to WHO <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: The ability of MRSA to resist methicillin can be due to the mecA gene, present in a mobile genetic element, SCCmec [8, 9], which encodes for a modified methicillintarget, PBP2a, with reduced affinity for β-lactam antibiotics [10].
text.formatted: The ability of MRSA to resist methicillin can be due to the mecA gene, present in a mobile genetic element, SCCmec <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>, which encodes for a modified methicillintarget, PBP2a, with reduced affinity for β-lactam antibiotics <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: A high genetic flexibility of S. aureus, enables easy development of novel defence mechanisms, yielding to new multi-resistant strains.
To manage the spread of AMR, the WHO identifies four pillars: prevention of infections, better access to health services, appropriate treatment, and accurate and fast diagnosis [11].
text.formatted: To manage the spread of AMR, the WHO identifies four pillars: prevention of infections, better access to health services, appropriate treatment, and accurate and fast diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Traditional antibiotic resistance diagnostics mainly involve the bacterial isolation and the performing of an Antibiotic Susceptibility Test.
This test is an official culture-based method where sensitivity to a given antibiotic is evaluated by an inhibition zone on agar plate.

However, this method is time-consuming, often taking three or more days needed for bacterial isolation and culture, and may fail, if the patient is already under an antibiotic treatment [12], or in the case that bacteria enter in viable but not cultivable (VBNC) state [13].
text.formatted: However, this method is time-consuming, often taking three or more days needed for bacterial isolation and culture, and may fail, if the patient is already under an antibiotic treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, or in the case that bacteria enter in viable but not cultivable (VBNC) state <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, traditional antibiotic tests delay targeted treatment and often necessitate initial use of broad-spectrum empirical therapies.
To limit the spread of MRSA and enable early administration of targeted antibiotics, the development of novel strategies for rapid and sensitive detection of resistant strains is urgently required.
Genotypic testing for mecA is widely used to rapidly optimize antimicrobial therapy in S. aureus infections.
Molecular-based techniques, such as Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), permit a faster detection, with response in less than a day.
However, PCR technique has high costs, requires trained staff, specific machines, and remains constrained to a lab-setting [14].
text.formatted: However, PCR technique has high costs, requires trained staff, specific machines, and remains constrained to a lab-setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: To address these drawbacks of PCR, isothermal amplification methods have been developed to accurately detect nucleic acids through faster amplification and easier adaptation to point-of-care format [15], since there is no need for temperature variations and specific hardware components such as a thermal cycler.
text.formatted: To address these drawbacks of PCR, isothermal amplification methods have been developed to accurately detect nucleic acids through faster amplification and easier adaptation to point-of-care format <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, since there is no need for temperature variations and specific hardware components such as a thermal cycler.

text.text: Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is one of the most promising isothermal techniques as it uses a set of 4 to 6 primers specific to the target gene and delivers results . within less than 1 hour [16].
text.formatted: Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is one of the most promising isothermal techniques as it uses a set of 4 to 6 primers specific to the target gene and delivers results . within less than 1 hour <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: When coupled with a colorimetric kit incorporating the pH-sensitive dye (such as Phenol Red), LAMP allows a naked-eye detection of amplification results, with a pink solution for a negative result and yellow for a positive result.
Here we present a LAMP assay for the sensitive detection of mecA within 25 min.
We designed and validated in silico novel LAMP primers targeting mecA.
After experimental validation using wellcharacterized S. aureus strains with or without the target gene, we applied the LAMP assays to screen clinical and foodborne S. aureus strains (Fig. S1).
text.formatted: After experimental validation using wellcharacterized S. aureus strains with or without the target gene, we applied the LAMP assays to screen clinical and foodborne S. aureus strains (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: The LAMP assay results were confirmed by the qPCR detection for the same gene, which corroborates efficiency and accuracy of the LAMP assay.
>Experimental
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Experimental</head>

text.text: Five well-characterized S. aureus strains were used for primer validation: USA300-JE2 [17], LAC [18] and COL [19], which hold mecA gene and are methicillin-resistant (referred to as MRSA), and RN-R [20], and Newman [21] which are methicillin-susceptible (referred to as MSSA).
text.formatted: Five well-characterized S. aureus strains were used for primer validation: USA300-JE2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, LAC <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> and COL <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>, which hold mecA gene and are methicillin-resistant (referred to as MRSA), and RN-R <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, and Newman <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> which are methicillin-susceptible (referred to as MSSA).

text.text: The isolation and identification of eight foodborne S. aureus strains from raw cow milk and pork meat, were previously described in detail [22].
text.formatted: The isolation and identification of eight foodborne S. aureus strains from raw cow milk and pork meat, were previously described in detail <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, starting from 150 mL of milk and 100 g of meat samples homogenized 1:2 in physiological solution, 10 mL were serially diluted and plated on Baird-Parker Agar supplemented with Egg Yolk Tellurire Emulsion (Oxoid, Milan, Italy).
After incubation at 37°C for 48 h, shiny, black colonies, with double halo were selected and streaked on Plate Count Agar (Oxoid, Milan, Italy) for purification.
S. aureus identification was performed by PCR targeting the species-specific thermonuclease nuc gene [23].
text.formatted: S. aureus identification was performed by PCR targeting the species-specific thermonuclease nuc gene <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Twenty-two clinical S. aureus strains were isolated from the blood from anonymized patient collected during sepsis diagnostic procedures and were kindly provided by Jean-Louis Herrmann (Hôpital Raymond Poincaré, Garches, France).
All strains were cultivated in Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth at 37°C.
An overnight culture was centrifuged at 8000 g, 4°C, for 10 min, and washed with TES buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 100 mM NaCl, 1.0 mM EDTA, pH of 7.8).
The bacterial pellet was lysed using FastPrep-24 (MP Biomedicals, France) with the following settings: 3 cycles of 20 sec at speed 4 m/sec, with 5 min rest between each cycle.
The genomic DNA (gDNA) was purified with the DNeasy blood and tissue kit (Qiagen, France).
Quantification of the gDNA was performed by NanoDrop2000 (ThermoScientific).
From these concentrations, the number of copies of the gene was calculated using the website NEBioCalculator from Biolabs with the following formula:
As mecA is a single-copy gene, we can approximate that one mecA DNA copy corresponds to one colony-forming unit (CFU).
The mecA gene sequence used for the LAMP primer design was extracted from the complete genome of S. aureus strain USA300JE2 (GenBank accession number NZ_CP020619), referred to as JE2.

Prior to primer design, mecA sequence was analysed using the Nucleotide Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) to assess the level of conservation of the target regions across different bacterial strains.
text.formatted: Prior to primer design, mecA sequence was analysed using the Nucleotide Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) (<ref type="url" target="https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi">https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi</ref>) to assess the level of conservation of the target regions across different bacterial strains.

text.text: LAMP primer sets were designed using the PrimerExplorer V5 program (https://primerexplorer.eiken.co.jp/lampv5e/index.html), targeting different sequences within the specific regions of the mecA gene.
text.formatted: LAMP primer sets were designed using the PrimerExplorer V5 program (<ref type="url" target="https://primerexplorer.eiken.co.jp/lampv5e/index.html">https://primerexplorer.eiken.co.jp/lampv5e/index.html</ref>), targeting different sequences within the specific regions of the mecA gene.

text.text: To minimize the risk of undesired secondary structures, such as hairpins, homodimers, and heterodimers, the primer sequences were analysed using the OligoAnalyzer software provided by Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT), available at https://eu.idtdna.com/pages/tools/oligoanalyzer.
text.formatted: To minimize the risk of undesired secondary structures, such as hairpins, homodimers, and heterodimers, the primer sequences were analysed using the OligoAnalyzer software provided by Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT), available at <ref type="url" target="https://eu.idtdna.com/pages/tools/oligoanalyzer">https://eu.idtdna.com/pages/tools/oligoanalyzer</ref>.

text.text: Designed LAMP sequences and locations on the mecA sequence are showed in Supplementary data (Table S1 and Fig. S2).
text.formatted: Designed LAMP sequences and locations on the mecA sequence are showed in Supplementary data (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: Thirty-eight sequences of Staphylococcus spp. mecA were extract from NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) with the following search: PBP2a family beta-lactam-resistant peptidoglycan transpeptidase MecA.
text.formatted: Thirty-eight sequences of Staphylococcus spp. mecA were extract from NCBI (<ref type="url" target="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/">https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/</ref>) with the following search: PBP2a family beta-lactam-resistant peptidoglycan transpeptidase MecA.

text.text: The sequences were aligned to highlight mismatch using Benchling (https://benchling.com/).
text.formatted: The sequences were aligned to highlight mismatch using Benchling (<ref type="url" target="https://benchling.com/">https://benchling.com</ref>).

text.text: The accession number of the sequences are provided in Table S2.
text.formatted: The accession number of the sequences are provided in Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>.

text.text: The qPCR primers were designed using Primer3 from Benchling.
The specificity to the target was verified by BLAST, and the absence of secondary structure was confirmed using ViennaRNA from Benchling.
For the amplification of mecA, the following primers were used: mecA3: 5' CCAATTCCACATTGTTTCGGTCTAA 3' [24] and qmecAR: 5' CCAGGAATGCAGAAAGACCAAAGCA 3'.
text.formatted: For the amplification of mecA, the following primers were used: mecA3: 5' CCAATTCCACATTGTTTCGGTCTAA 3' <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> and qmecAR: 5' CCAGGAATGCAGAAAGACCAAAGCA 3'.

text.text: Primers were first validated by PCR using FIREPol DNA Polymerase Kit (Solisbiodyne, France).
The reaction mix was composed of the FIREPol buffer BD X1, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM dNTP, 0.3 µM of each primer, 0.05 U/µL of FIREPol, for a total volume of 20 µL.

The thermocycler Nexus GX2 (Eppendorf, France) was programmed for a first denaturation step of 95°C for 4 min, then 35 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 17 sec, annealing at 60°C for 35 sec and extension at 72°C for 1 min.
Then a final extension was performed at 72°C for 10 min. qPCR was performed using the Luna Universal qPCR master mix from New England Biolabs (France).
The reaction mix was composed of qPCR buffer X1, 0.3 µM of each primer for a total volume of 20 µL.

The reaction was performed using qPCR StepOne Plus (Applied Biosystem, France) which was programmed for a first denaturation step of 95°C for 20 sec, then 40 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 3 sec, annealing and extension at 60°C for 30 sec.
A final step includes a denaturation of 15 sec and an annealing/extension of 1 min.
A melting curve was then performed to check the specificity by increasing 0.5°C every 15 sec until reaching 95°C.

The LAMP reactions were performed with WarmStart LAMP Kit (DNA & RNA) for the Fluorimetric LAMP reaction, and with WarmStart Colorimetric LAMP 1X Master Mix (DNA & RNA) for colorimetric LAMP reaction (NewEngland Biolabs, France).
text.formatted: The LAMP reactions were performed with WarmStart LAMP Kit (DNA & RNA) for the Fluorimetric LAMP reaction, and with WarmStart Colorimetric LAMP 1X Master Mix (DNA & RNA) for colorimetric LAMP reaction (NewEngland Biolabs, France).

text.text: Each reaction mixture contained 20 μL of reagents, including WarmStart LAMP 1x Master Mix, 1x LAMP primer mix (16 μM FIP and BIP, 2 μM F3 and B3, and 4 μM of the LF and LB), fluorescent dye 50X for fluorometric assays, 2 μL of DNA sample and nuclease-free water.
Reactions were performed using the StepOne Plus system.
All detection assays were performed in duplicate (technical replicates), and ultrapure water and gDNA of methicillin-sensitive strains were used as templates in negative controls.

Products of the amplification were validated by loading in 2% agarose gel with ethidium bromide solution (Invitrogen, France) and running in electrophoresis unit Mupid One (Eurogentec) for 30 min at 135 V. The gel is then visualized with E-Box Gel documentation (Vilber, France).
Adult bovine serum (CliniSense, France) was selected as model biological matrix and was used without further processing.
S. aureus JE2 and RN-R cells from overnight BHI cultures were harvested, washed three times with TES buffer, and used to spike the two matrices.
Bacterial cells were incubated in these media under gentle agitation at room temperature for 1 h.
Cells were then lysed using FastPrep.
The LAMP reaction was performed using 2 µL of clarify lysates.
Agar spot diffusion method was performed to test susceptibility of S. aureus isolates to methicillin.

S. aureus cells from an overnight BHI liquid culture were spread evenly on a ø6 mm petri-dish with Mueller-Hinton (MH) agar using sterile beads, and then 5 µg of methicillin sodium salt (Sigma, France) were dropped in the centre of the plate.
Following the incubation at 37°C for 24 h, the diameter of zone of inhibition was measured.
>Results and discussion
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results and discussion</head>

text.text: Primers in the LAMP assay were designed to target a highly prevalent mecA gene among MRSA [25].
text.formatted: Primers in the LAMP assay were designed to target a highly prevalent mecA gene among MRSA <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Five primer sets (Table S1) were screened for their specificity by conducting BLAST searches (Fig. S1), that indicated their high specificity to the mecA target.
text.formatted: Five primer sets (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>) were screened for their specificity by conducting BLAST searches (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>), that indicated their high specificity to the mecA target.

text.text: The primer sets were also validated for selfdimerization and hetero-dimer formation by using OligoAnalyzer.
In silico alignment with mecA sequence from non-aureus Staphylococci validated a high conservation rate of the gene among Staphylococcus spp.
(Fig. S3).
text.formatted: (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: To select the best primer set we used gDNA of the MRSA strain JE2 and of the methicillin-sensitive S. aureus strain RN-R as a negative control.
The amplification was recorded in a plate using a 10 ng/µL of gDNA and a fluorescent reporter.
Typical sigmoidal amplification curves were observed in the reaction wells and result showed that the primer sets ID4 and ID16 accelerated the LAMP assay compared to other primers (Fig. 1a).
text.formatted: Typical sigmoidal amplification curves were observed in the reaction wells and result showed that the primer sets ID4 and ID16 accelerated the LAMP assay compared to other primers (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: The primer sets ID4 and ID16 enabled perceptible result for JE2 after a 25-to 30-min, meanwhile no effective amplification was detected at this time, using gDNA of RN-R (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: The primer sets ID4 and ID16 enabled perceptible result for JE2 after a 25-to 30-min, meanwhile no effective amplification was detected at this time, using gDNA of RN-R (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: Amplification of the negative controls have been observed with a delay in fluorometric LAMP.
To validate 25-min reaction time, the amplification has been performed with colorimetric LAMP assay using MRSA JE2, MSSA RN-R and no template control for 25 min, 30 min, 35 min and 40 min (Fig. S4).
text.formatted: To validate 25-min reaction time, the amplification has been performed with colorimetric LAMP assay using MRSA JE2, MSSA RN-R and no template control for 25 min, 30 min, 35 min and 40 min (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S4</ref>).

text.text: Only the tube with JE2 turned to yellow at 25 and 30 min, while negatives RN-R and NTC slightly turned to yellow at 40 min, confirming the 25-min reaction time.

The weak late amplification, that sometimes occurs in LAMP assays, reflects an intrinsic property of LAMP reactions, which can produce nonspecific signals if the reaction extends beyond the optimized time [16, [26] [27] [28].

text.text: Further verification of the specificity of the primer sets ID4 and ID16, included the cross reactivity between well-characterized S. aureus strains holding mecA gene and sensitive S. aureus strains (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: Further verification of the specificity of the primer sets ID4 and ID16, included the cross reactivity between well-characterized S. aureus strains holding mecA gene and sensitive S. aureus strains (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: The same concentration of gDNA (10 ng/µL) for each bacterial strain was used to evaluate the colorimetric read-out.
The reaction mixtures changed colour from pink to yellow within 25 min, indicating the amplification, while no colour change was observed with negative controls (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: The reaction mixtures changed colour from pink to yellow within 25 min, indicating the amplification, while no colour change was observed with negative controls (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: When the reaction mixtures were loaded onto the gel, their electrophoretic bands confirmed the specificity of the primer sets ID4 and ID16 (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: When the reaction mixtures were loaded onto the gel, their electrophoretic bands confirmed the specificity of the primer sets ID4 and ID16 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: Interestingly, a clear amplification was observed with S. aureus LAC strain that holds one mismatch in mecA sequence (position 1271, C to T) (Fig. S3).
text.formatted: Interestingly, a clear amplification was observed with S. aureus LAC strain that holds one mismatch in mecA sequence (position 1271, C to T) (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: To verify the optimal amplification temperature of the LAMP assay, we used gDNA from JE2 MRSA (10 ng/µL) and the primer set ID16, to perform reactions at various temperatures (63-66 °C, with 1°C intervals).
Amplification was observed at all tested temperatures (Fig. S5).
text.formatted: Amplification was observed at all tested temperatures (Fig. <ref type="figure">S5</ref>).

text.text: Ultimately, 65 °C, the temperature recommended by the LAMP kit supplier, was selected as the optimal amplification temperature, and was further used.

To determinate the limit of detection (LoD) of the established LAMP assay, serial 10-fold dilutions (ranging from 1.5 pg to 1.5 fg of gDNA/µL) were tested using the primer sets ID4 and ID 16 (Fig. 2).

text.text: Colorimetric assay indicated LoD of 1.5 pg gDNA/µL (corresponding to ca. 500 copies of mecA/µL) and 15 fg gDNA/µL (ca. 5 copies of mecA/µL) using the primer sets ID4 and ID16, respectively (Fig. 2a, b).

text.text: These LoD values were confirmed when the LAMP assay was coupled with the fluorescent read-out (Fig. 2c, d).

text.text: Since the lower LoD was obtained with the primer set ID16 (ca. 5 copies of mecA/µL), this set was further use.
Since there is one copy of mecA gene in the S. aureus genome, the calculated LoD of the assay is 5x10 3 CFU/mL.
For comparison, when the amplification was performed by qPCR, using JE2 strain, the LOD of 1 pg/µL of gDNA (corresponding to 340 mecA copies/µL) was obtained (Fig. S6).

text.text: The qPCR standard curve had a good linear correlation between the DNA concentration and the Ct value (R² = 0.995), indicating that the developed qPCR assay was reliable and could quantify the target sequence.
However, the LAMP assay was more rapid, easier to perform and lower in cost.
Therefore, LAMP is more suitable for quantitative analysis of samples with low target concentrations.
Furthermore, the low LoD of our LAMP assay is comparable with values obtained for mecA detection using other LAMP assay as listed in Table 1, recently proposed in the literature.

text.text: To further evaluate the developed colorimetric LAMP assay, we applied it on food and clinical S. aureus isolates and compared the results with the qPCR, as illustrated in Fig. 3a.

text.text: Eight S. aureus strains isolated from raw meat and milk samples were first tested for their susceptibility to methicillin.
Overnight bacterial solutions were diluted and plated on MH solid medium, and methicillin (5 µg) was spotted in the center of plates, which were incubated and photographed.

Four strains showed resistance (milk isolates 227, 228, and meat isolates 303, 304), while others (milk isolates 219, 220, and meat isolates 301, 302) were susceptible and showed well-defined zones of inhibition (Fig. S7).
text.formatted: Four strains showed resistance (milk isolates 227, 228, and meat isolates 303, 304), while others (milk isolates 219, 220, and meat isolates 301, 302) were susceptible and showed well-defined zones of inhibition (Fig. <ref type="figure">S7</ref>).

text.text: To verify whether the observed β-lactam resistance was mecA-mediated, the qPCR analysis was performed.
As shown in Fig. 3b, all resistant samples showed the amplification of mecA gene.
text.formatted: As shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3b</ref>, all resistant samples showed the amplification of mecA gene.

text.text: In the LAMP assay, 4 food samples testing positive by the two conventional microbiological methods were also positive as colour of their solution changed from pink to yellow (Fig. 3b).
text.formatted: In the LAMP assay, 4 food samples testing positive by the two conventional microbiological methods were also positive as colour of their solution changed from pink to yellow (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3b</ref>).

text.text: When methicillin susceptibility test was performed on S. aureus blood isolates, 6 out of 22 strains had well defined inhibition zone, without apparition of resistant colonies inside the zone, and were identified as MRSA (Fig. S8). qPCR confirmed that all 6 resistant strains possess the mecA gene (Fig. 3c).

text.text: A pink-to-yellow colour change was observed with the same 6 out of 22 isolates when tested using the developed LAMP assay (Fig. 3c).
text.formatted: A pink-to-yellow colour change was observed with the same 6 out of 22 isolates when tested using the developed LAMP assay (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3c</ref>).

text.text: Results of the colorimetric LAMP assays were confirmed by running the reaction products on a 2% agarose gel (Fig. S9).
text.formatted: Results of the colorimetric LAMP assays were confirmed by running the reaction products on a 2% agarose gel (Fig. <ref type="figure">S9</ref>).

text.text: Overall, our LAMP assay correctly identified both mecA-positive and mecA-negative samples in food and clinical isolates, with 100% specificity (correct positive and negative results relative to the total number of tests performed), as confirmed by the reference method, qPCR (Table S3).
text.formatted: Overall, our LAMP assay correctly identified both mecA-positive and mecA-negative samples in food and clinical isolates, with 100% specificity (correct positive and negative results relative to the total number of tests performed), as confirmed by the reference method, qPCR (Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Bovine serum samples spiked with JE2 or RN-R strains was analysed under optimized conditions to evaluate the matrix effect on overall analytical performance (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: Bovine serum samples spiked with JE2 or RN-R strains was analysed under optimized conditions to evaluate the matrix effect on overall analytical performance (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: Both colorimetric and fluorescent detections clearly distinguished between mecA-positive and mecA-negative strains when performed directly on bacterial lysates without DNA purification, as shown in Figs. 4b and 4c.
text.formatted: Both colorimetric and fluorescent detections clearly distinguished between mecA-positive and mecA-negative strains when performed directly on bacterial lysates without DNA purification, as shown in Figs. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4b</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4c</ref>.

text.text: This finding demonstrating the robustness of the developed method.
We successfully developed a LAMP assay for the detection of the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant S. aureus strains.
The specificity of newly designed LAMP primers was confirmed in silico against mecA gene sequences from other non-S. aureus staphylococci.

The colorimetric and fluorometric LAMP assay enabled reliable identification of mecA-positive genomic DNA samples through a simple procedure: direct mixing of the target DNA with the reaction solution and incubation at 65 °C for 25 minutes.
In addition to its rapid turnaround time, the assay exhibited excellent performance in terms of limit of detection (5 copies/µL) and specificity (100%).

These characteristics directly address the limitations of conventional PCR-based methods and highlight the potential of LAMP for use in point-of-care settings, where rapid and accessible diagnostics are essential.
Using both food and clinical S. aureus isolates, we demonstrated that the specificity of the LAMP assay was comparable to qPCR.
However, unlike qPCR, the LAMP assay was significantly easier to perform and more cost-effective.
Furthermore, the robustness of the assay was validated in complex matrices serum and milk, where direct mechanical lysis was used and no significant inhibition was observed in colorimetric assay.
The developed LAMP assay, thus, offers a scalable and cost-effective solution for decentralized diagnostics.
Taken together, these findings show that the developed LAMP assay provides a practical, scalable, and affordable solution for decentralized and point-of-care diagnostics in a timely manner.
